blocks.content: A file system is not just a bucket of files sitting loose on a disk. It organizes them into a navigable hierarchy of directories, what most people simply call folders, and the exact shape of that hierarchy has changed several times across the history of operating systems, each version fixing a real limitation in the one before it.

This chapter builds up that history in order, starting from the simplest possible directory design and ending at the tree structured, link supporting model almost every modern system actually uses, along the way covering absolute and relative paths, and the frequently confused difference between a hard link and a symbolic link.
1. A Directory Is Just a Special File
blocks.text: 1. A Directory Is Just a Special File

blocks.content: The single most important idea in this entire chapter is that a directory is not some fundamentally different kind of object from a file. At the OS level, a directory is really just a file whose content happens to be a table of entries, and each entry maps a name to a reference, typically an inode number, pointing at either another file or another directory.

This is why directories can be nested arbitrarily deep: a directory entry pointing at another directory is exactly as valid as one pointing at a regular file, since both are ultimately just references stored in a table. The operating system treats the two cases specially when displaying or interpreting them, but the underlying storage mechanism is identical.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409068765-568002537.png
blocks.alt: A Directory Is Just a Special File

blocks.title: The one insight to keep
blocks.content: A directory is a file containing a table of name to reference mappings. Everything else in this chapter is really just different ways of arranging and connecting those tables.
2. Single Level Directory

The earliest and simplest possible design keeps exactly one flat directory for the entire system. Every file that exists anywhere lives in this one table, with no subfolders and no per user separation at all.

The appeal is obvious: there is nothing to design, no traversal logic, no nested lookups. The real limitation shows up almost immediately once more than one person or program uses the system: since every file lives in the same single table, no two files anywhere on the entire system can share a name. Two different users both wanting to save a file called report.txt is simply not allowed.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409068765-756634153.png
3. Two Level Directory

The next design gives each user their own separate directory, nested one level below a system root. This solves the cross user naming collision immediately: alice and bob can each have their own report.txt, since each name only needs to be unique within its own user directory, not across the whole system.

The limitation that remains is organizational, not about naming collisions between users. Within a single user own directory, everything is still flat. A user with hundreds of files has no way to group related ones into meaningful sub categories, every single file sits in that one user level table regardless of what it actually is.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409068766-976906021.png
4. Tree Structured Directory

The standard modern answer removes the flat limitation entirely by letting directories contain other directories, forming an actual tree. A user can create as many nested subdirectories as they like, docs inside their home directory, pics inside that, project folders inside docs, arbitrarily deep, and organize files by whatever structure actually makes sense to them.

This tree structure is what essentially every general purpose operating system in use today, Linux, macOS, Windows, actually implements. A single root directory sits at the top, and every other file and directory in the system is reachable by following some path down through the tree from that root.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409068766-488514814.png
5. Absolute and Relative Paths

Once files live in a tree, there needs to be a way to describe where in that tree a particular file sits, and there are exactly two ways to do it. An absolute path always starts from the tree root and fully specifies a location no matter where the caller currently happens to be. A relative path is interpreted starting from the current working directory instead, and only makes sense in that context.

Concretely, /home/alice/docs/report.txt is an absolute path: it works identically regardless of what the current directory happens to be at the moment. But if the current working directory is already /home/alice, the same file can also be reached with the much shorter relative path docs/report.txt, which would resolve to a completely different, likely nonexistent location if typed from anywhere else.

6. Acyclic Graph Directory: Letting One File Live in Two Places
blocks.text: 6. Acyclic Graph Directory: Letting One File Live in Two Places

blocks.content: A pure tree has one real limitation left: every file can only be reached through exactly one path, since a tree by definition has exactly one route from the root to any given node. Sometimes that is genuinely too restrictive, a file that two different projects both legitimately need can only physically exist inside one of those project folders under a pure tree.

An acyclic graph directory structure relaxes this by allowing the same underlying file to be referenced from more than one directory location, without actually duplicating its data anywhere. The mechanism that makes this possible in real systems is links, and the next section covers the two very different kinds in real depth.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195021-273734522.png
blocks.alt: Acyclic Graph Directory: Letting One File Live in Two Places

blocks.content: 7. Hard Links vs Symbolic Links

A hard link is literally another directory entry pointing at the exact same underlying inode as an existing file. There is nothing that distinguishes a hard link from the original name, both are simply entries in some directory table that happen to point at the same inode number, completely indistinguishable from each other at the file system level.
Symbolic links add a layer of indirection
blocks.text: Symbolic links add a layer of indirection

blocks.content: A symbolic link, also called a soft link, works completely differently. It is a small, separate special file whose own content is simply a path string pointing at another file. Reading through a symbolic link requires the file system to first read that path string, then look up whatever it points to, one extra level of indirection that a hard link never needs.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-79065918.png
blocks.alt: Symbolic links add a layer of indirection

blocks.content: This structural difference has a very real, very concrete consequence when the original file gets deleted. Deleting the original name behind a hard link changes nothing for the other hard link, since the underlying data was never actually removed, only one of possibly several names pointing at it disappeared. Deleting the original behind a symbolic link leaves that symbolic link dangling, pointing at a path that no longer resolves to anything.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-272960436.png
blocks.alt: Symbolic links add a layer of indirection

A hard link is another name for the same file. A symbolic link is a separate file that only remembers a path.
8. Why True Cycles Are Avoided

An acyclic graph deliberately stops short of allowing genuine cycles, a directory that somehow, through some chain of links, ends up containing one of its own ancestors. If that were allowed, a program walking the whole directory tree, to list every file for a backup, for instance, could loop forever, following the cycle around and around with no way to know it had already visited that point.

Real systems handle this in one of two ways: most simply disallow hard links to directories entirely, permitting them only for regular files, which makes a directory cycle structurally impossible to create in the first place. Systems that do allow directory links add explicit cycle detection during traversal instead.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-781712127.png

blocks.title: Why most systems just say no
blocks.content: Rather than adding cycle detection everywhere a directory might be traversed, most file systems sidestep the entire problem by simply forbidding hard links to directories. Symbolic links to directories are still allowed, since a dangling or looping symbolic link can be detected and reported without corrupting the underlying tree structure itself.

10. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Confusing a hard link with a symbolic link, and specifically not knowing what happens to each one when the original file is deleted, a hard link keeps working, a symbolic link goes dangling.","Assuming directories are a fundamentally different kind of object from files at the OS level, when conceptually a directory is itself just a specially interpreted file containing a table of entries.","Believing a symbolic link and its target must live on the same disk or file system, when a symbolic link is just a path string and can point anywhere, including across file systems, unlike a hard link.","Forgetting that a tree structure only allows one path to any given file, which is exactly the limitation that hard and symbolic links exist to relax."]
items: Confusing a hard link with a symbolic link, and specifically not knowing what happens to each one when the original file is deleted, a hard link keeps working, a symbolic link goes dangling.
Assuming directories are a fundamentally different kind of object from files at the OS level, when conceptually a directory is itself just a specially interpreted file containing a table of entries.

Believing a symbolic link and its target must live on the same disk or file system, when a symbolic link is just a path string and can point anywhere, including across file systems, unlike a hard link.
Forgetting that a tree structure only allows one path to any given file, which is exactly the limitation that hard and symbolic links exist to relax.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain precisely what happens when the original file behind a hard link versus a symbolic link is deleted, this exact distinction is one of the most commonly asked systems interview questions, and most confident sounding wrong answers get exactly this part backwards.

Every time a path is typed, from a simple relative filename to a long absolute path, it is being resolved down through exactly the kind of directory table structure this chapter walked through, one name to reference mapping at a time, all the way from the root to the file itself.
